newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cites cut in drug money shipments to Colombia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cites cut in drug money shipments to Colombia.

text.p: A senior U.S. official said on Tuesday a federal effort in New York to block drug money from being sent to Colombia by some money transfer agents has cut their laundering by 30 percent in the past seven months.
Treasury Under Secretary for Enforcement Raymond Kelly told a House of Representatives banking subcommittee money transmissions to Colombia had been running at about $800 million a year.

To account for that amount, he said, each Colombian household in New York would have to send $30,000 a year to Colombia through money agents. Since the households' median income was $27,000 a year, he added, "there was cause for concern."

Treasury's Geographic Targeting Order programme requires small, non-bank transmitters who deal mainly with immigrants who send money back home to report on senders and recipients of cash purchases for transmissions of $750 or more. Officials said many of these transmitters are small operators licensed by major money transfer companies and operating out of neighbourhood stores.
They did not name the companies allegedly involved.

"The GTO caused an immediate and dramatic reduction in the flow of narcotics proceeds to Colombia through New York City money transmitters," Kelly said. He added that while the agency review of results continued, "the targeted money transmitters' overall business volume to Colombia appears to have dropped by approximately 30 percent."
Kelly said he thought most of the money had shifted from New York area agents to other East Coast cities or was smuggled in bulk out of the United States.

"We have observed a dramatic increase in customs interdiction and seizure activity at the airports, seaports, common carriers and highways along the East Coast -- over $50 million since the GTO went into effect," he said. This was about four times higher than in prior years, he told the subcommittee.

At the same time that there were fewer transmissions of more than $750 there was a doubling of transmissions of under $750, but transmitters were being arrested for intentionally structuring deals to violate the $750 limit, he said.
